1	# Audience divergence — the live crowd vs the trip planners
2	
3	EdFringeNow now points at two decisions with two front ends: *Fringe Discover*
4	(the mobile-first home site, "what can I make right now") and the planner at
5	`/plan` (desktop-first, "which of my favourites can I catch, on which dates").
6	This page exists to hold the evidence that **the two do not reduce to one set of
7	requirements** — where they pull apart, where they actively conflict, and the
8	narrow spine they genuinely share.
9	
10	It is research, not requirements: nothing here is a decision. The requirements
11	implication (two tracks rather than one) is for a human to promote into
12	`product-wiki/product-requirements/`.
13	
14	## Key insights
15	
16	- The two surfaces do not reduce to one set of requirements. That is the finding.
17	- The planner packs the day; the evidence says a good day is half empty.
18	- One sold-out flag: a fact for the live surface, a decaying guess for the planner.
19	- Live asks the user for nothing. The planner needs a CSV from a third-party extension.
20	- "When should I come?" has no live version — and no competitor answers it.
21	- What they truly share is small: the catalogue, the travel model, the promise.
22	- The plan-to-live handover is the one shared feature worth building. It does not exist.
23	
24	## The two crowds in a line each
25	
26	- **Live, in-festival.** On the ground in Edinburgh during 7–31 August, deciding
27	  for the next hour or two. A third of the Fringe audience lives in Edinburgh and
28	  has no trip to plan at all; most ticket buyers buy a single ticket.
29	- **Trip planners.** Two thirds of the audience come from outside Edinburgh,
30	  choose dates and beds, and assemble a favourites list months before August —
31	  the 2026 programme launched on 4 June, and audiences now engage with the
32	  festival long before it starts.
33	
34	They may be the same person in different states — the Fringe CEO's "rule of
35	thirds" describes one visitor pre-planning about a third of their time and
36	leaving the rest open. That does not make it one requirement set; it makes the
37	handover between the two surfaces a design problem in its own right.
38	
39	## Where they diverge
40	
41	| Axis | Live surface | Planner |
42	|---|---|---|
43	| **Horizon** | the next 1–2 hours | a stay chosen weeks out, then re-tuned |
44	| **Origin** | device location, "here, now" | no useful location; an accommodation base at best |
45	| **Taste input** | zero-effort defaults, genre chips, free/paid | an explicit favourites list built elsewhere, at high effort |
46	| **Correctness** | is this *still* catchable — a live fact | will this *be* catchable — a forecast that decays |
47	| **Objective** | one good, reachable option now | a whole trip's worth, and which dates make it possible |
48	| **Cost of error** | a wasted walk, a late entrance | non-refundable tickets, travel and beds booked around a wrong plan |
49	| **Device & context** | phone, outdoors, one hand, sunlight, patchy signal | desktop, indoors, deliberate, wide canvas |
50	| **Time to value** | seconds; typing is failure | minutes of deliberate work is acceptable |
51	| **State** | stateless — the answer expires with the hour | persistent — favourites, window, itinerary, exports (CSV/ICS) |
52	| **Season** | only 7–31 August, and value shifts across the run | February–July, peaking after each programme drop |
53	| **Success** | "I chose something and I made it" | "N of my favourites got caught, and the days were liveable" |
54	
55	## Requirements that actively conflict
56	
57	These are the places where satisfying one crowd well makes the other worse.
58	Naming them is the point of this page.
59	
60	1. **Pack the day vs leave the day open.** The planner's allocator is an
61	   earliest-finish-first greedy — it maximises the number of shows placed. The
62	   audience evidence points the other way: two to three shows a day is the pace
63	   commonly advised, visitors who combined structured planning with open time
64	   reported higher satisfaction than over-schedulers, and the rule of thirds asks
65	   for roughly a third of the time planned. A planner that fills the day
66	   optimally also destroys the gaps the live surface serves. The two surfaces can
67	   be jointly optimal only if the planner's objective is *not* "maximum shows".
68	2. **Live truth vs planning truth, from one catalogue.** Both surfaces read the
69	   same `data/normalized/shows.json`. For the live surface, sold-out /
70	   started-already is a *fact* and staleness is the core failure mode. For the
71	   planner, the same field is a *forecast* about a date weeks away, which decays
72	   in the opposite direction (shows sell out as August approaches; walk-ups are
73	   easy in week one and scarce in weeks two and three). Identical data, two
74	   incompatible honesty obligations — the planner arguably must show "may sell
75	   out before you book" where the live surface must show "gone".
76	3. **Zero input vs high-effort input.** The brief's live target is "a brand-new
77	   user with zero taps already sees useful results". The planner's front door is
78	   a CSV export the user produces on another site — and, as far as the research
79	   shows, via a third-party browser extension. One surface's core virtue is
80	   asking nothing; the other's is asking for something quite hard to obtain.
81	4. **Personalisation model.** Live personalisation is coarse taste (ten festival
82	   genres, free/paid) applied to whatever is reachable. Planner personalisation
83	   is an explicit, already-curated favourites set — a different data model, a
84	   different privacy posture (the planner keeps parsed favourites in
85	   `localStorage` for three days; the live surface keeps nothing), and different
86	   recommendation logic. Merging them into "one personalisation system" would
87	   serve neither.
88	5. **What "optimise" even means.** Live: maximise the chance the user goes and
89	   enjoys one show inside a slack budget. Planner: maximise favourites caught
90	   across a window — and, upstream of that, choose the window. The planner's
91	   *most valuable* question ("when should I come?") has no live analogue at all,
92	   and no profiled competitor answers it.
93	6. **Which constraints are even visible.** The live surface's binding constraint
94	   is travel time to the next commitment. The planner's real binding constraint
95	   may not be shows at all: over half of would-be attendees reportedly could not
96	   find affordable accommodation within a 90-minute commute, so dates are chosen
97	   against beds. `/plan`'s "pick my best dates" scores windows purely on show
98	   catchability — optimising a variable the user may not be free to move.
99	7. **Failure of the map.** Live, a map answers "where is that relative to me".
100	   In the planner, there is no "me" — the map's job becomes clustering and
101	   walkability across a day, which is a different visualisation with different
102	   requirements (and the reason the planner's schedule draws travel legs rather
103	   than a map).
104	
105	## What the two genuinely share
106	
107	Small, and worth keeping small deliberately:
108	
109	- **One catalogue and one venue geometry** — the scraped `shows.json` /
110	  `venues.json`, already shared, plus the haversine + per-mode travel model in
111	  `plan/lib/travel.js` and the `UK_BOUNDS` helper both front ends import.
112	- **Honesty about data gaps** — no ticket prices beyond free/paid, no live seat
113	  counts beyond a sold-out flag. Neither surface may imply data we don't have.
114	- **The same emotional promise** — the overwhelm lifting. 37% of audiences
115	  reported struggling to pick a show; both surfaces exist to answer that, at
116	  different distances from the decision.
117	- **A handover, in one direction.** The planner's deliberate gaps are the live
118	  surface's demand. Nothing today connects them (no shared favourites, no "your
119	  plan says you're free until 19:00"), and that connection is the one place where
120	  a *shared* requirement would be justified.
121

136	## Open questions
137	
138	- **Is the shared person real, or two populations?** No evidence found either way
139	  on how many planner users are also in Edinburgh mid-festival. If the overlap is
140	  large, the handover (plan → live) is the highest-value unbuilt feature; if it
141	  is small, the two products should probably diverge further, not converge.
142	- **What should the planner optimise for?** "Most shows placed" is contradicted
143	  by the satisfaction evidence, but "leave a third open" has no measured optimum
144	  either. What does a *good* Fringe day look like, quantitatively?
145	- **How does availability actually decay between planning and August?** Nothing
146	  cited yet on sell-out rates by week or by show popularity — which decides how
147	  honest the planner can be about a plan made in June.
148	- **Does the accommodation constraint dominate date choice?** If it does, date
149	  scoring needs a second input the product doesn't have.
150	- **Is there a third crowd?** Artists, reviewers and industry are all in the same
151	  data with different needs (own-show scheduling, review runs); nothing here has
152	  looked at them.
153	- **Does the divergence extend to the scraper?** The live surface wants frequent
154	  refresh of status for today; the planner wants a stable whole-festival
155	  snapshot. Whether one data pipeline serves both well is unexamined.

1	# Competitor landscape
2	
3	How people discover and schedule Edinburgh Fringe shows today, and how each
4	existing tool handles — or ignores — the two questions EdFringeNow is built
5	around: *"what can I actually make right now?"* (the home site, Fringe Discover)
6	and *"which of my favourites can I actually catch, on which dates?"* (the planner
7	at `/plan`). Compiled once, refined in place.
8	
9	The field is not one field. The live/in-the-moment side has essentially one
10	incumbent; the planning side is crowded, and got noticeably more crowded for
11	2026.
12	
13	## Key insights
14	
15	- Nobody does live reachability. "Nearby now" stops at close and starting soon.
16	- The official app plans better than we assumed — calendar sync, offline, 200k downloads.
17	- Clash-free, travel-aware scheduling is table stakes. Plan My Fringe shipped it years ago.
18	- Three claims are unclaimed: import my favourites, pick my dates, and the other seven August festivals.
19	- Fringe Finder plans around what is still on sale. That is the axis we are behind on.
20	- Half Price Hut tickets are in person only — live supply no app can see.
21	- Nobody here has used any 2026 rival. All of it is compiled from their own marketing.
22	
23	## The incumbents
24	
25	### Official Edinburgh Fringe app
26	
27	The Fringe Society's own app browses and books the full programme and serves
28	**both** of our questions — one weakly, one properly.
29	
30	- Closest to Fringe Discover: **"Nearby now"**, which uses phone location to show
31	  shows near you that are starting soon, plus **"shake to search"** for a random
32	  suggestion. Every published description of the feature (the official page,
33	  press coverage, the app-store listing, the build agency's case study) still
34	  frames it as *proximity + starting soon*. None mentions travel mode, travel
35	  time, or the user's **next commitment** — the slack calculation. No description
36	  of the 2026 edition claims otherwise.
37	- On the planning side it is stronger than this page previously recorded: **My
38	  Planner** saves shows by date and **syncs them to the user's own calendar**,
39	  alongside e-ticket QR codes, an **offline mode** for saved performances and
40	  tickets, and notifications when the next show starts.
41	- Reach: the build agency's case study reports downloads **surpassing 200,000** —
42	  a distribution no independent tool in this field is likely to match.
43	
44	The 2026 edition was again due to download in July 2026.
45	
46	### Plan My Fringe
47	
48	A schedule **optimiser**, and the closest existing thing to `/plan`. Its current
49	feature list overlaps ours almost item for item: a wishlist with per-show
50	ratings, then a schedule packing in as many shows as it can while honouring
51	**maximum budget**, **maximum shows per day**, **minimum gap between shows**,
52	**average walking speed**, and **minimum lunch, evening meal and sleep times**.
53	Its **"Fringe Trail"** chains shows to minimise walking and waiting and can be
54	viewed as an animated route on Google Maps; the website and app share one
55	wishlist, schedule and preferences; a **Recommendations** section (and a
56	"Fringey" chat) suggests shows using AI.
57	
58	What it does *not* appear to do: start from the user's **edfringe.com favourites
59	export**, or answer **"which dates should I come?"** — it optimises within a visit
60	the user has already decided on. That, rather than clash-free scheduling, is
61	where `/plan`'s remaining distinctness sits.
62	
63	### edfringe.com programme, filters and favourites
64	
65	The canonical catalogue, with filters (date/time, genre, free) and a personal
66	favourites list — strong for planning ahead, weak for the spontaneous "near me,
67	right now, still reachable" question. Favourites are the input `/plan` consumes;
68	extracting them as CSV is served by a **third-party Chrome extension** ("EdFringe
69	Favourites to CSV", maintained per festival year), not by any documented native
70	export.
71	
72	### Half Price Hut
73	
74	Same-day and next-morning **half-price** tickets, browsable online but purchasable
75	**in person only** at the Fringe Box Office (opening 12 August in 2026). A
76	price/spontaneity channel rather than a discovery-by-reachability tool — and a
77	reminder that a slice of live supply never appears in any app's inventory.
78	
79	### Reviews & word of mouth
80	
81	Outlets such as **ThreeWeeks**, plus star ratings on posters and Royal Mile
82	flyering, drive a large share of in-festival choice; discovery is heavily social
83	and serendipitous. Around 4,300 professional reviews were uploaded to edfringe.com
84	in 2025.
85	
86	## The 2026 planner-side field
87	
88	Several independent tools aimed squarely at the trip-planning crowd surfaced for
89	2026. None was profiled in this wiki's first pass, and together they change the
90	read on where the gap is.
91	
92	- **[Plan Your Fringe](https://planyourfringe.com/)** — "checks every single show
93	  against your dates, taste and budget and builds your day-by-day itinerary";
94	  free, independent, about two minutes end to end, itinerary downloadable as a
95	  PDF. Direct overlap with `/plan`'s output, without the favourites import.
96	- **[Fringe Finder](https://fringe-finder.netlify.app/)** — browse every 2026
97	  show, **track ticket availability**, and plan days with an **AI assistant** that
98	  builds a day-by-day plan from what is *still on sale*; describes itself as an
99	  official festival pilot (unverified). Availability-aware planning is the piece
100	  most tools skip — and the one axis where we are behind rather than ahead.
101	- **[Fringe Planner / edfringemap.com](https://edfringemap.com/)** — every show on
102	  one interactive map, filterable by day, genre, area, price and start time, then
103	  book. The closest thing to Fringe Discover's *map* surface, though as a
104	  browse-and-filter map rather than a reachability calculation.
105	- **[Ed Fringe Guide](https://edfringeguide.com/index.html)** and **[Another
106	  Fringe Guide](https://www.anotherfringeguide.com/)** — unofficial show finders /
107	  browsers, comedy-leaning.
108	- **[Edinburgh Fringe Planner](https://edfringeplanner.co.uk/)** — a further
109	  independent planner surfaced in the same sweep, not yet examined.
110	
111	## The cross-festival field (almost empty)
112	
113	Every tool above is a *Fringe* tool. The city runs eight overlapping festivals in
114	August, and only one profiled competitor spans them:
115	
116	- **[Data Thistle](https://edinburghfestival.datathistle.com/)** — combined
117	  listings across the Fringe, International, Book, Jazz, Tattoo, Art, Film, Free
118	  Fringe, Free Festival and Fringe by the Sea, plus a commercial events API. A
119	  listings directory rather than a planner: no reachability, no itinerary, no
120	  favourites. The closest thing found to a multi-festival competitor.
121	- The **[Edinburgh Festivals Listings API](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/projects)**
122	  publishes a gallery of 13 apps built on it — Plan My Fringe, FringeFlow,
123	  TicketBadger, Frindr, myFestival, Festival Clock, Fringe Vibes and others.
124	  The data covers all 11 festivals; almost every app on it is named and framed
125	  around the **Fringe alone**. Nobody in the gallery claims cross-festival
126	  planning.
127	
128	Two caveats on how strong that reads. The gallery blurbs are the only evidence —
129	nobody here has used these tools, and the gallery may simply be stale. And a
130	cross-festival tool would not necessarily be *listed* there, since the API is not
131	the only source. Treat "the cross-festival claim is unclaimed" as the current
132	best reading, not a settled finding.
133	
134	## Where the gaps are
135	
136	**Live reachability — still open.** No tool centres full reachability: location
137	_plus_ travel mode/time _plus_ next-commitment slack ("can I see this and still
138	make my 7pm?"). The official app's "Nearby now" remains the nearest neighbour and
139	stops at proximity + starting-soon; Plan My Fringe models walking time, but for a
140	pre-curated plan. That live calculation is still Fringe Discover's distinct
141	position — see the product brief (`docs/product-spec.md`).
142	
143	**Planning — crowded, and the moat is narrower than it looks.** Clash-free,
144	travel-aware, meal-break-aware scheduling with per-day limits is **table stakes**
145	on this side of the field: Plan My Fringe has shipped all of it for years, and
146	2026 added at least two more itinerary builders. What no profiled competitor
147	does:
148	
149	1. start from the user's **existing favourites list** rather than making them
150	   re-pick shows inside the tool; and
151	2. answer **"when should I come?"** — scoring date windows across the whole
152	   festival, the decision a visitor makes *before* any scheduling question
153	   exists.
154	
155	Those two, not the scheduler, are what a planner-side requirement set would rest
156	on. They are also a different claim from the live surface's, which is why the two
157	surfaces should not be reasoned about as one product — see
158	[audience-divergence/](../audience-divergence/README.md).

1	# Market & audience
2	
3	The scale of the Edinburgh Fringe and the audience behaviour EdFringeNow is built
4	for. Two decisions live here, not one: the in-the-moment "what can I make right
5	now" (the home site, *Fringe Discover*) and the weeks-earlier "which shows, which
6	dates" (the planner at `/plan`). Compiled once, refined in place.
7	
8	## Key insights
9	
10	- 3,649 Fringe shows across 258 venues in 2026 — plus ~900 more events from seven other August festivals.
11	- 37% of people struggle to pick a show. Two thirds buy just one ticket.
12	- 78% come to see something they would not normally — they want surprise, not better filters.
13	- A third of the audience lives in Edinburgh. Two thirds travel in and plan months ahead.
14	- The advice everyone gives is: do not fill the day. Two or three shows.
15	- Beds may pick the dates, not shows — over half cannot find an affordable room nearby.
16	- Nobody has data on how people choose in the street. Not us, not anyone.
17	
18	## Scale
19	
20	### 2026 festival (running 7–31 August 2026)
21	
22	- **3,649 shows** across **258 venues**, **53,884 performances**, artists from
23	  **71 countries** — announced at the programme launch on 4 June 2026.
24	- Genre split at launch: **1,401 comedy**, **1,025 theatre**, **168 musicals and
25	  opera**.
26	- Smaller than 2025 on both counts (3,893 shows / 301 venues), and still two
27	  orders of magnitude more than any one visitor can see.
28	
29	### 2025 festival (latest full ticket data)
30	
31	- **3,893 shows** across **301 venues**, **53,942 performances**, artists from
32	  **62 countries**.
33	- **~2.6 million tickets** issued (2,604,404) — roughly flat on 2024, still below
34	  the 2019 pre-pandemic peak of about 3 million.
35	- **edfringe.com took over 3 million visits and 37 million page views**, and
36	  ~4,300 professional reviews were uploaded to the site to help audiences choose.
37	
38	*(2025's ticket figures stay on this page because they remain the newest
39	issued-ticket data — the Fringe Society publishes each year's ticket and audience
40	data after the festival closes, so 2026's cannot land before late August 2026.)*
41	
42	This scale is the product premise: the official programme is a catalogue that
43	rewards planning ahead and overwhelms the person deciding in the moment.
44	
45	### The Fringe is not all of August
46	
47	The page's scale figures — and the product built on them — cover one festival.
48	Seven others run concurrently: the International Festival (147 performances),
49	the Military Tattoo (nightly), the Deaf Festival (80+ events), the Film Festival
50	(38 features), the Art Festival (40+ mostly-free exhibitions), the Book Festival
51	(~600 events) and Fringe by the Sea. Roughly 900 further events, overlapping the
52	Fringe almost completely in time and largely in place.
53	
54	That changes the overwhelm problem's shape rather than only its size. The Fringe
55	is ~80% of August's events, so any relevance- or proximity-ranked list shows a
56	Fringe-only city; and the non-Fringe events are the *scarcer* ones — a Fringe
57	show plays ~25 times, a Book Festival author appears once. The programme's scale
58	buries exactly what cannot be seen twice. Dates, counts, locations, the six
59	different shapes an "event" takes across these festivals, and whether the data is
60	obtainable are all worked through on
61	[festival-season/](../festival-season/README.md).
62	
63	## The overwhelm / decision problem
64	
65	Fringe Society audience data puts numbers on it:
66	
67	- **37% of audiences struggled to pick a show** to go and see.
68	- **Two thirds of ticket buyers bought only one ticket** — for most of the
69	  audience the Fringe is a single decision, not a curated run of shows.
70	- **78% came to the Fringe to see something they wouldn't go and see otherwise** —
71	  the appetite is for discovery, not for a known quantity.
72	
73	The standard advice around that, consistent across guides and relevant to both
74	surfaces:
75	
76	- With more than 3,800 shows, choosing "can feel like a daunting task"; the
77	  advice is to lean on filters, star ratings and reviews, and to **embrace
78	  serendipity** — the show you'd never have booked is often the one people still
79	  talk about.
80	- **Leave travel time.** Edinburgh is compact but August streets are not; guides
81	  repeat that venues which look close together are not close in August — the
82	  reachability constraint Fringe Discover makes first-class rather than an
83	  afterthought.
84	- **Two to three shows a day** is the pace commonly advised as comfortable —
85	  leaving room to eat, walk, and stand still.
86	- **Don't fill the day.** Fringe CEO Tony Lankester's "rule of thirds" — about a
87	  third of the time pre-planned, the rest left open — alongside reporting that
88	  visitors who combined structured planning with open time were more satisfied
89	  than those who over-scheduled.
90	
91	That last point is load-bearing here: the gaps a planner deliberately leaves are
92	exactly the gaps the live surface exists to fill.
93	
94	## Two crowds, not one
95	
96	This page previously described a single audience (the in-the-moment one) because
97	it was seeded from the *Fringe Discover* brief. The repo now ships two front
98	ends — the mobile-first home site and the desktop-first planner at `/plan` — and
99	they serve different people, or the same people in different states.
100	
101	### A. Live, in-festival — "what can I make right now"
102	
103	- **On the ground, deciding for the next hour or two.** Location, travel mode and
104	  the next commitment are the constraints; the catalogue is noise.
105	- **A third of the audience lives in Edinburgh** — locals have no trip to plan and
106	  no accommodation to book, and decide close to the moment by construction.
107	- **Same-day supply is a real channel, and an in-person one.** The Half Price Hut
108	  sells same-day (and next-morning) tickets from the Fringe Box Office only — not
109	  online, not in the app — opening 12 August in 2026, 10:00–18:00 daily.
110	- **Walk-up availability is not constant across the run.** Guides report walk-ups
111	  are easy in the opening week and that by weeks two and three popular shows —
112	  comedy headliners especially — sell out days in advance. The live surface's
113	  usefulness therefore moves with the calendar as well as the hour.
114	- **How the decision is actually made in the street is undocumented.** Posters,
115	  Royal Mile flyering, star ratings and word of mouth clearly drive a large share
116	  of it, but practitioners writing about Fringe marketing state plainly that
117	  nobody knows what works — there is no measured breakdown of in-the-moment
118	  discovery channels to cite.
119	
120	### B. Trip planners optimising around favourite shows
121	
122	- **Two thirds of the audience come from outside Edinburgh** — they choose dates,
123	  book beds and travel, and assemble a show list long before August.
124	- **Audiences now engage months ahead.** Reporting on how the Fringe audience has
125	  changed describes a 2026 audience that follows artists online, votes in polls
126	  and treats the festival as a live-entertainment marketplace well before August —
127	  a marked shift from the "turn up and grab a flyer" Fringe of a decade ago.
128	- **Accommodation binds *which dates* a trip can happen**, not as a footnote:
129	  coverage of the festival's accommodation crisis reports over half of people
130	  hoping to attend could not find an affordable place to stay within a 90-minute
131	  commute. Dates get chosen against beds as much as against shows — something the
132	  planner's "pick my best dates" currently ignores.
133	- **The favourites list is the planner's raw material, and it lives elsewhere.**
134	  Shows are favourited on edfringe.com and saved in the official app's *My
135	  Planner* (which syncs to a personal calendar). Getting that list *out* as a CSV
136	  is served by a third-party Chrome extension ("EdFringe Favourites to CSV",
137	  updated per festival year); no native edfringe.com CSV export is documented.
138	  The planner's front door depends on an export path we do not own.
139	- **The programme launch is the season's starting gun.** The 2026 programme went
140	  live on 4 June 2026, with shows revealed in batches from 11 February — so
141	  planning demand exists for months before any live demand can.
142	
143	### The same person, at different hours
144	
145	These are not necessarily two populations. The rule-of-thirds advice describes one
146	visitor who pre-plans part of a day and leaves the rest open; the planner serves
147	that first third and the live surface the other two. What differs is not identity
148	but **state** — horizon, device, inputs, and what "correct" even means. Those
149	differences are worked through on their own page:
150	[audience-divergence/](../audience-divergence/README.md). Nothing on this page
151	should be read as implying one merged requirement set.
152	
153	## Audience segments (product-brief hypotheses)
154	
155	From the product brief (`docs/product-spec.md`, an internal hypothesis not yet
156	externally validated): visitors mid-festival on foot without a fixed plan; people
157	with a _gap_ between commitments; locals and tourists intimidated by the
158	programme's size. Decisive in the moment rather than researchers, with an
159	emotional target of "delight + relief."
160	
161	Those segments describe crowd **A** only — the brief predates `/plan`, and no
162	equivalent written segmentation exists for the trip-planning crowd. The partial
163	external evidence for crowd B is the block above (two thirds non-resident,
164	months-ahead engagement, accommodation-first date choice); a validated
165	segmentation for either crowd remains an open question.

1	# The Edinburgh festival season
2	
3	Everything else happening in Edinburgh alongside the Fringe — the other August
4	festivals, the rest of the summer, and the seasonal things that are not
5	festivals at all. Compiled once, refined in place.
6	
7	This page exists because the product's premise ("3,649 shows is too many") is
8	only true of one festival. In August the city runs at least eight programmes
9	concurrently, and they are not variations on the Fringe: they differ in scale by
10	two orders of magnitude, in how an event behaves in time, in whether a ticket
11	exists, and in whether the data is reachable at all.
12	
13	## Key insights
14	
15	- August is at least eight overlapping festivals, not one — the Fringe is ~80% of the events and all of the noise.
16	- One free API already carries all 11 festivals, with coordinates, start times, durations and prices.
17	- That API has no sold-out field — our sharpest live signal does not survive a move off the Fringe scraper.
18	- Its licence bars redistributing dumps to third parties, and we commit our data to a public repo.
19	- "An event" is six different shapes: daily run, short season, one-off, nightly anchor, drop-in, all-day occasion.
20	- The Art Festival is 40+ mostly-free drop-in exhibitions with no start time — a shape nothing in the product models.
21	- Summer starts in June: Hidden Door, the Meadows, the Carnival and Jazz & Blues all finish before the Fringe opens.
22	
23	## The August cluster (2026)
24	
25	Eight programmes overlap almost completely. Every one of them is running on
26	15–19 August; a visitor in the city that week is inside all of them at once
27	whether they know it or not.
28	
29	| Festival | Dates | Scale | Where |
30	|---|---|---|---|
31	| **Festival Fringe** | 7–31 Aug | 3,649 shows / 53,884 performances / 258 venues / 71 countries | citywide |
32	| **International Festival (EIF)** | 7–30 Aug | 147 performances / 44 countries / 2 exhibitions | a few large halls |
33	| **Royal Edinburgh Military Tattoo** | 7–29 Aug (not Sundays) | one show, ~800 performers, ~9,000 seats a night, ~230,000 a year | one venue |
34	| **Edinburgh Deaf Festival** | 7–16 Aug | 80+ events | Deaf Action + Fringe venues |
35	| **International Film Festival (EIFF)** | 13–19 Aug | 38 new features, 21 world premieres | 5–6 cinemas + pop-up |
36	| **Art Festival** | 14–30 Aug | 40+ exhibitions, 25+ partner galleries, mostly free | galleries citywide |
37	| **International Book Festival** | 15–30 Aug | ~600 events / ~600 writers / 41 countries | one campus, 3 rooms |
38	| **Fringe by the Sea** | 31 Jul–9 Aug | a small Fringe of its own | **North Berwick, not Edinburgh** |
39	
40	Two things fall out of the table:
41	
42	- **Volume is overwhelmingly Fringe.** Every non-Fringe August festival added
43	  together is roughly 900 events against the Fringe's 3,649 shows. Any ranking
44	  that sorts purely on relevance or proximity will show a Fringe-only city.
45	- **Scarcity runs the other way.** A Fringe show typically plays ~25 times. A
46	  Book Festival author appears once. An EIFF screening is often a single
47	  showing. The events that are hardest to replace are the ones the volume
48	  ranking buries.
49	
50	**Free Fringe (4–30 Aug) and Free Festival (6–30 Aug)** are not separate
51	festivals for data purposes — they are producers whose shows appear inside the
52	Fringe programme, so the existing catalogue already contains them.
53	
54	**Edinburgh Summer Sessions** (24–29 Aug per a listings aggregator, not yet
55	confirmed against a promoter source) is an outdoor concert series rather than a
56	festival programme, and is listed here only so a later pass knows it was
57	considered.
58	
59	## The rest of the summer
60	
61	The season starts in June and the pre-August festivals are almost entirely free
62	and outdoor — a materially different offer from the ticketed August cluster.
63	
64	| Event | Dates (2026) | Shape |
65	|---|---|---|
66	| **Hidden Door** | 3–7 Jun | pop-up arts festival, The Paper Factory |
67	| **Meadows Festival** | 6–7 Jun | free community weekend, one park |
68	| **International Children's Festival (Imaginate)** | May–Jun | children's theatre |
69	| **Jazz & Blues Festival** | 17–26 Jul | 100–170+ concerts (sources differ), clubs to concert halls |
70	| **Edinburgh Festival Carnival / Multicultural Festival** | 19 Jul | one-day city-centre parade |
71	| **Folk & Food Festival** | 24 Jul–2 Aug | free-entry food and folk, George Square Gardens |
72	
73	Outside the summer entirely, and named only so they are not re-researched:
74	Science Festival (April), Beltane Fire Festival (30 April), Storytelling
75	Festival (October), Hogmanay (December).
76	
77	## The seasonal city that is not a festival
78	
79	The brief's user — someone with a free hour — is not only choosing between
80	shows. Guide coverage of an Edinburgh summer converges on the same non-ticketed
81	list: Arthur's Seat and Holyrood Park, the Royal Botanic Garden, Inverleith
82	Park, the Meadows, Princes Street Gardens, Portobello beach (swimming), the
83	Water of Leith walkway, and the Saturday markets (Stockbridge, Grassmarket,
84	Castle Terrace).
85	
86	Two honest caveats:
87	
88	- **This is guide-site material, not a dataset.** There is no listings feed for
89	  "the Meadows is nice in August." Anything the product does here is a
90	  hand-curated short list, and should be sized accordingly.
91	- **The repo already has the seam.** `js/places.js` geocodes arbitrary
92	  non-show destinations through Nominatim, so a curated seasonal place is
93	  representable today without new infrastructure.
94	
95	## What "an event" means differs per festival
96	
97	This is the finding that matters most for design, and it is not a branding
98	question. Across the eight August programmes an event behaves in one of six
99	ways in time, and the differences change what the product can truthfully
100	promise:
101	
102	1. **Run** — repeats near-daily at one time across a long run (Fringe, Fringe by
103	   the Sea). Missing it today costs nothing.
104	2. **Short season** — a handful of dated performances, often at differing times
105	   (EIF theatre/opera/dance, larger Deaf Festival work). Each date is scarce.
106	3. **One-off** — happens exactly once (Book Festival author events, most EIFF
107	   screenings, Jazz concerts, talks). Missing it is terminal.
108	4. **Nightly anchor** — the same show every night, one venue, huge capacity,
109	   sold months ahead (the Tattoo). Behaves like a fixed commitment, not a
110	   candidate.
111	5. **Drop-in** — no start time at all: opening hours and a duration the visitor
112	   chooses (Art Festival exhibitions, typically ~10:00–17:00, mostly free).
113	6. **All-day occasion** — a single dated outdoor thing with no seat and no slot
114	   (the Carnival parade, Meadows Festival, Folk & Food).
115	
116	Only shape 1 is modelled today. Shapes 3 and 5 are the ones that break existing
117	assumptions hardest: a one-off is a point rather than a lane, and a drop-in has
118	no start time to reach in time for.
119	
120	## Locations
121	
122	- **The Fringe is citywide** (258 venues); everything else is concentrated.
123	- **The Book Festival is effectively one campus** — Edinburgh Futures Institute
124	  (1 Lauriston Place), plus McEwan Hall and, new for 2026, Greyfriars Kirk. All
125	  within a few minutes' walk of each other and of the Fringe's Bristo Square
126	  cluster.
127	- **EIF uses a handful of large halls** — Usher Hall, Festival Theatre, The
128	  Queen's Hall, Church Hill Theatre. Church Hill is the outlier, ~25 minutes
129	  south of the centre on foot.
130	- **EIFF spreads deliberately** — Cineworld Fountainbridge, Filmhouse, Cameo,
131	  Monkey Barrel, plus **Leith Theatre** (a genuine 30+ minute walk from the Old
132	  Town) and a pop-up screen at the National Gallery.
133	- **The Tattoo is the Castle Esplanade**, which also means the top of the Royal
134	  Mile is congested nightly.
135	- **Fringe by the Sea is in North Berwick**, ~25 miles east — a train journey,
136	  not a walk. Any travel estimate that treats it as a city venue is wrong by an
137	  order of magnitude.
138	
139	## Can we actually get the data?
140	
141	Yes, and better than expected — with two sharp edges.
142	
143	### The Edinburgh Festivals Listings API
144	
145	`api.edinburghfestivalcity.com`, run by Festivals Edinburgh Limited, originally
146	built by the Science Festival in 2016. It is the **official** listings database
147	for all 11 major festivals and is **free to use** with a registered access key.
148	
149	- **Coverage.** The `festival` parameter accepts `fringe, demofringe, jazz,
150	  book, international, tattoo, art, hogmanay, science, imaginate, film, mela,
151	  storytelling`. The status page confirms 2026 data is loaded for the
152	  Children's, Science, Tattoo, Film, International, Jazz, Fringe, Art and Book
153	  festivals.
154	- **Fields we need are present.** Events carry `festival`, `title`, `genre`,
155	  `genre_tags`, `artist`, `country`, `description`, images, a venue record with
156	  `latitude`/`longitude`, wheelchair access, and a `performances[]` array of
157	  `{start, end, duration_minutes, price, concession, price_string,
158	  is_at_fixed_time}`. Query parameters include lat/lon/distance, date range,
159	  price range, genre, venue and `modified_from` for incremental sync.
160	- **`is_at_fixed_time` is the drop-in flag** — the API already distinguishes a
161	  timed performance from an open-hours one, which is exactly the shape
162	  distinction the product needs.
163	- **It carries real prices.** The edfringe GraphQL API deliberately does not
164	  (only `priceType` flags); the Listings API returns `price` and `price_string`.
165	  This would close a limitation the product brief currently apologises for.
166	
167	**Edge 1 — no availability.** The performance object has no sold-out, on-sale or
168	remaining-tickets field. The Fringe scraper's `ticketStatus` has no counterpart
169	here, so for non-Fringe festivals the product cannot honestly say whether a
170	ticket exists. Anything that implies parity would be inventing data.
171	
172	**Edge 2 — the licence bars redistributing dumps.** Commercial use is explicitly
173	permitted and attribution is required (a visible credit plus a link to the API).
174	But developer users "must not redistribute listings to third parties by means of
175	either data feeds or data dumps", and applications must refresh at least every
176	24 hours. This repo currently **commits its normalized catalogue to a public git
177	repo and serves it as a static JSON file from GitHub Pages** — a pattern that
178	needs an explicit answer from Festivals Edinburgh before it is used with their
179	data. It is the one genuine blocker found.
180	
181	**Edge 3 — Fringe data specifically is approval-gated and link-restricted**
182	(found 2026-07-31 in the ticketing pass): developers build against a randomised
183	`demofringe` dataset and must [submit the app for review](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/fringe_approval)
184	before live Fringe access; the Fringe terms require that show links go **only to
185	edfringe.com** — "not… any other ticketing site, including the venue's own
186	site". Sync is near-real-time (`modified_from`, "a delay of a few minutes"), and
187	a beta [MCP endpoint](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/mcp)
188	exists. The full ticketing/provider picture is on
189	[fringe-ticketing/](../fringe-ticketing/README.md).
190	
191	### Keeping the Fringe on its own source
192	
193	The existing edfringe GraphQL scraper stays the better Fringe source: it carries
194	per-performance `ticketStatus`, the 104-label subgenre taxonomy, content
195	warnings and age guidance the Listings API does not expose at the same fidelity.
196	The realistic architecture is two adapters into one normalized schema, not a
197	migration.
198	
199	### Other aggregators
200	
201	**Data Thistle** (`edinburghfestival.datathistle.com`) publishes combined
202	listings across the Fringe, International, Book, Jazz, Tattoo, Art, Film, Free
203	Fringe, Free Festival and Fringe by the Sea, and sells an events API — evidence
204	that cross-festival listings are a real product, and the closest thing found to
205	a direct multi-festival competitor.
206	
207	The Listings API's own project gallery lists 13 apps built on it (Plan My
208	Fringe, FringeFlow, TicketBadger, Frindr, myFestival, Festival Clock, Fringe
209	Vibes and others). Notably, nearly all of them are named and framed around the
210	**Fringe** despite the API carrying all 11 festivals — no listed project claims
211	cross-festival planning as its point. That gap is unverified beyond the gallery
212	blurbs and belongs in the competitor page once someone actually uses them.

250	
251	- **Does the licence permit our static-file architecture?** The one blocker.
252	  Committing Listings API data to a public repo and serving it as a JSON file
253	  from GitHub Pages may read as redistributing a data dump. Needs a direct
254	  answer from Festivals Edinburgh, not an inference from the terms page.
255	- **What does the API actually return?** Every field claim here comes from the
256	  documentation, not from an authenticated response — nobody has registered a
257	  key. (Narrowed 2026-07-31: the public explorer confirms 2026 Fringe data is
258	  loaded, and the per-performance field list was verified against the events
259	  documentation; per-festival event counts and `is_at_fixed_time` population
260	  remain unchecked.)
261	- **Is `is_at_fixed_time` enough to derive event shape?** It separates timed from
262	  drop-in, but not one-off from run from nightly. Those may be derivable by
263	  counting performances per event — unconfirmed.
264	- **Does the API carry the Deaf Festival?** It is not in the `festival`
265	  parameter list, and its events are produced with the Fringe — so they may
266	  appear under `fringe` with no distinguishing marker, which would make the
267	  festival invisible in a festival filter.
268	- **Jazz & Blues event count.** Sources say "over 170 performances", "more than
269	  100 concerts" and "over 150 concerts" — no authoritative figure found.

272	  "help people see the diversity of Edinburgh" goal rests on an unmeasured
273	  assumption that they would if they knew.

275	  ships, who maintains it and how does it stay true?

1	# Fringe ticketing & providers
2	
3	Who actually sells an Edinburgh Fringe ticket, who all the venue operators
4	("providers") are, whether a third party can sell tickets itself, and whether
5	any provider or aggregator feed could replace scraping edfringe.com. Compiled
6	once, refined in place.
7	
8	This page exists to answer a specific owner question — *"are edfringe.com and
9	edfest.com both just fronts for the event organizers?"* — and the answer turned
10	out to be half yes: one of the two is exactly that, and it is not the one the
11	product depends on.
12	
13	## Key insights
14	
15	- edfringe.com is an independent charity's box office, not the venues' — the venues' own storefront is edfest.com.
16	- Every ticketed show must give the Fringe box office at least 25% of its tickets; venues sell the rest themselves.
17	- One vendor, Red61, powers ten of the fifteen biggest operators' box offices. Provider access is one Red61 question.
18	- Nobody offers an affiliate or agent scheme — not the Society, not the venues. Deep links earn nothing, anywhere.
19	- Our own scrape is the provider census: 24 operator families cover 83% of the programme; the tail is 171 small venues.
20	- The official Listings API bans linking to any ticket seller except edfringe.com — even the venue's own site.
21	- Only the edfringe GraphQL has availability for the whole programme. The scrape cannot be retired.
22	
23	## Who actually sells a Fringe ticket
24	
25	The premise to correct first: **edfringe.com is not a front for the venue
26	operators.** It is run by the [Edinburgh Festival Fringe Society](https://www.oscr.org.uk/about-charities/search-the-register/charity-details?number=SC002995),
27	an independent registered Scottish charity (SC002995, income £8.28m FY2024)
28	governed by an open **£5/year membership** that elects its board — structurally
29	separate from the operators, and [publicly feuded with](https://www.scotsman.com/whats-on/arts-and-entertainment/edinburgh-festival-fringe-longest-running-venue-operator-says-he-has-lost-confidence-in-the-fringe-society-3791322)
30	by them at times. The Society performs no curation (open access: anyone with a
31	show, a willing venue and the registration fee is in the programme) and runs the
32	central box office.
33	
34	**The allocation model** is the load-bearing mechanic, from the Society's own
35	[participant guidance](https://help.registration.edfringe.com/create-or-edit-a-show/payout-and-fringe-allocation.aspx):
36	every ticketed show must allocate a **minimum 25% of tickets per performance**
37	to the Fringe Box Office (sliding scale above that), on which the Society takes
38	**5%+VAT commission**; the venue sells the remainder through its own box office
39	at its own rate ([Assembly charges 4%+VAT](https://s3.eu-west-2.amazonaws.com/cdn.assemblyfestival.com/Assembly%20Festival%202026%20Information%20Pack%20for%20Performers%20(6).pdf);
40	[Summerhall 8%](https://www.summerhallarts.co.uk/wp-content/uploads/2025/01/Summerhall-Arts-Festival-Information-Pack_2025_web.pdf),
41	and reports that ~70% of its tickets nonetheless sell through the Fringe box
42	office). This model is why the scrape's `NO_ALLOCATION_CONTACT_VENUE` status
43	exists: when the Society's allocation for a performance is exhausted, [the
44	official advice](https://www.edfringe.com/faqs/) is to check with the venue box
45	office — the ticket may still exist, just not in the channel we can see. In the
46	2026 data that status marks 1,279 of ~59,900 performances (2.1%), concentrated
47	at the big operators.
48	
49	**Platforms:** since March 2025 edfringe.com runs on an interim site built by
50	Australian agency equ on its Tikketr platform (the GraphQL the scraper hits;
51	the [official app](https://play.google.com/store/apps/details?id=com.tikketr.edfringe.prod&hl=en)
52	is `com.tikketr.edfringe.prod` and takes [~30% of all ticket sales](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/our-digital-transformation-strategy-march-2025/)).
53	[Red61 ran the Society box office 2009–2023](https://www.red61.com/news/red61-celebrates-20-years-at-the-edinburgh-festival-fringe/)
54	and still powers the venue side (17 federated VIA instances in 2024). A
55	permanent replacement site is being [built by Storm ID for Fringe 2027](https://www.edfringe.com/about-us/news-and-blog/fringe-society-appoints-storm-id-to-develop-new-website-for-the-fringe/) —
56	meaning **the scraper's target platform is explicitly interim**.
57	
58	## edfest.com — the venues' own storefront
59	
60	The other half of the owner's premise is correct. [edfest.com](https://edfest.com/about)
61	is operated by **Showcatcher Ltd** ([company 07628569](https://find-and-update.company-information.service.gov.uk/company/07628569/officers),
62	lead director William Burdett-Coutts — Assembly's founder and artistic
63	director): a cross-venue storefront formed by the major operators — Assembly,
64	C ARTS, Gilded Balloon, Just the Tonic, Pleasance, Underbelly, ZOO (Summerhall
65	was an eighth founder and has left the list). It explicitly
66	[acts "as an agent on behalf of multiple venues and producers"](https://edfest.com/faqs)
67	on Red61 rails, sells only participating venues' shows in one basket, caps
68	booking fees at £5, and fronts the [Love the Fringe membership](https://theqr.co.uk/2026/06/04/edfest-2026-launch-fringe-crisis-how-to-save-on-tickets/).
69	So the accurate map: **edfringe.com = the charity's central box office;
70	edfest.com = the big operators' joint venture; venue sites = each operator's
71	own channel** — three parallel channels selling overlapping inventory.
72	
73	(Also answered: **Edinburgh Playhouse** is an [ATG receiving house](https://www.atgtickets.com/venues/edinburgh-playhouse/),
74	not a Fringe operator — but it *is* [registered Fringe venue 59](https://www.edfringe.com/tickets/venues/edinburgh-playhouse)
75	in 2026, hosting four big ATG-ticketed comedy one-nighters.)

131	## Can we sell tickets ourselves? No — and nobody can
132	
133	The verified negative, adversarially checked: **no open affiliate, agent,
134	reseller, white-label or purchase-API route into Fringe ticketing exists.**
135	
136	- The **Fringe Society** offers no scheme of any kind; its
137	  [ticketing T&Cs](https://tickets.edfringe.com/terms-and-conditions) bar using
138	  tickets "for any commercial, business or re-sale purposes", and its current
139	  Tikketr platform has no public partner API at all.
140	- **No venue operator** advertises an affiliate or agent programme. The big
141	  operators channelled exactly this energy into their own closed joint venture —
142	  edfest.com — rather than opening a channel to outsiders.
143	- The **platform layer** has the technology but not the access:
144	  [Spektrix runs a dedicated Agency API](https://integrate.spektrix.com/docs/agentguide)
145	  (third-party agents buying on a credit agreement the venue sets up per-agent)
146	  and [Red61 VIA offers APIs, white-label sales and cross-selling](https://www.red61.com/ticketing-solutions/) —
147	  but in every case access is granted per-client under a negotiated commercial
148	  agreement. No self-service signup, no published rates.
149	- Existing "third-party sellers" prove the pattern: See Tickets and Ents24
150	  retail [The Stand's own club shows](https://www.seetickets.com/venue/the-stand-comedy-club/8933)
151	  under explicit venue agency deals; TodayTix and Fever carry **no** actual
152	  Edinburgh Fringe inventory (London transfers and previews only); LivingSocial
153	  retails Love the Fringe *memberships*, not tickets. New for 2026, a
154	  [Sold Out Board lottery pilot](https://www.theticketingbusiness.com/2026/07/west-end-style-lottery-ticketing-system-coming-to-edinburgh-fringe/)
155	  resells last tickets for sold-out shows at face value — also a closed
156	  arrangement.
157	
158	Bottom line for this product: "selling tickets ourselves" would mean separate
159	negotiated agent agreements with dozens of operators across at least five
160	ticketing platforms, with no published programme to even apply to. The realistic
161	ceiling is **deep links to each seller — which earn nothing**, because no
162	commission scheme exists anywhere in the Fringe ecosystem. (This kills the
163	hoped-for ticket-affiliate revenue path; `shared/affiliates.js` stays a
164	travel/accommodation monetisation seam only.)
165	
166	## Can anything replace the edfringe scrape? Mostly no
167	
168	- **The official [Edinburgh Festivals Listings API](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation)**
169	  is the only licensed catalogue alternative: free, official, same registered-show
170	  universe, per-performance start/end/price, a near-real-time
171	  `modified_from` sync ("a delay of a few minutes"), 2026 Fringe data loaded,
172	  and a beta [MCP endpoint](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/mcp).
173	  But Fringe access is **approval-gated** (build against a randomised
174	  `demofringe` dataset, [submit the app for review](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/fringe_approval)),
175	  it has **no availability/sold-out field**, and its licence adds a sharp rule:
176	  [links for Fringe shows must go to edfringe.com only](https://api.edinburghfestivalcity.com/documentation/fringe_approval) —
177	  "not… any other ticketing site, including the venue's own site". An
178	  API-approved product could not deep-link to venue box offices.
179	- **Venue operators:** probed directly, the big operators publish nothing
180	  machine-readable (Assembly: locked CMS; Gilded Balloon: WordPress with no
181	  event type; Pleasance/Underbelly/The Stand: server-rendered HTML; Monkey
182	  Barrel: Wix). Two real exceptions, found and verified by live fetch:
183	  **Traverse** exposes a fully public
184	  [Spektrix v3 JSON API](https://system.spektrix.com/traverse/api/v3/events)
185	  including **live per-performance seat availability** (a fetched 2 Aug 2026
186	  performance returned `available: 19, capacity: 302`), and **Summerhall Arts**'
187	  festival site has an open [WordPress REST API with events and performances](https://festival.summerhallarts.co.uk/wp-json/wp/v2/types).
188	  Together they cover ~94 of 4,100 shows — real, but not a strategy.
189	- **Aggregators:** [Data Thistle](https://www.datathistle.com/what-we-do/for-listings-suppliers/)
190	  has genuine full-Fringe coverage but is paid, contact-for-pricing; Skiddle's
191	  API is beta and non-commercial-only with thin coverage; WeGotTickets,
192	  Eventbrite and Ents24 carry effectively nothing.
193	
194	**The verdict:** for the full programme *with availability* — the thing the Now
195	page's honesty depends on — **the edfringe GraphQL scrape has no replacement.**
196	The defensible end-state is: official Listings API as the licensed catalogue
197	backbone *if* its approval and linking rules are acceptable, with a slimmed
198	edfringe probe kept solely as the availability overlay — or simply keep the
199	scrape as-is, knowing its platform is interim (Storm ID site lands for 2027, so
200	the scraper breaks on that timetable regardless).

242	- **Would the Listings API approve us, and on what terms?** Whether Fringe
243	  approval would be granted to a product that also shows availability badges
244	  scraped from edfringe.com — and whether blending the two sources in one

1	# Festival cities beyond Edinburgh
2	
3	Which other cities in the world carry the Edinburgh-in-August pattern — many
4	overlapping festivals, thousands of temporary show runs and exhibitions, and a
5	city swarming with visitors who have to *choose*. This page exists because the
6	product's premise (overwhelm + reachability) is a property of that pattern, not
7	of Edinburgh, so anywhere the pattern recurs is a candidate market. It ranks
8	candidates by how close they are **structurally** (does the same mechanism
9	produce the overwhelm?) rather than by fame. Compiled once, refined in place.
10	
11	## Key insights
12	
13	- Adelaide is the only real peer, and still less than half of Edinburgh: 1,648 shows to 3,649.
14	- Avignon OFF is the closest structural twin — 1,780 open-access shows in 141 theatres inside one walled town.
15	- 300+ fringes exist worldwide, but only three sell more than 250,000 tickets.
16	- Edinburgh has a free official cross-festival listings API. No other festival city found has an equivalent.
17	- Avignon and Montreal break the English-only assumption before any other candidate does.
18	- Adelaide spreads over 562 venues — a compact walkable centre is an Edinburgh quirk, not a fringe property.
19	- Milan's Fuorisalone is the same shape in another art form: 1,100+ events across 16 districts.
20	
21	## What "another Edinburgh" actually means
22	
23	Edinburgh's August is not one festival. Eleven major festivals share the city
24	across the year, and in August the Fringe (7–31 Aug 2026), the International
25	Festival (7–30), the Tattoo (7–29), the Art Festival (14–30), the Book Festival
26	(15–30) and the International Film Festival (13–19) overlap, with the densest
27	window around 14–25 August.
28	
29	Underneath that, the thing that actually generates the overwhelm is the Fringe's
30	**open-access** model: anyone who finds a room and pays a registration fee is
31	listed, so supply is uncapped and the city converts itself into venues. Scale
32	figures for the Fringe itself live on
33	[market-and-audience/](../market-and-audience/README.md) — 3,649 shows across 258
34	venues in 2026, ~2.6m tickets in 2025.
35	
36	Three distinct mechanisms produce an Edinburgh-shaped city, and they matter
37	separately because each implies a different data and product problem:
38	
39	1. **Open access** — uncapped supply, one registration fee, thousands of parallel
40	   runs. This is the mechanism EdFringeNow is built against.
41	2. **A curated core with an unofficial "off"** — a ticketed official programme
42	   plus a sprawling satellite ecosystem the official body does not list.
43	3. **A festival *season*** — many discrete, separately-run festivals stacked
44	   back-to-back in one city, rather than one festival with thousands of shows.
45	
46	A fourth, weaker pattern — **long temporary exhibition runs** (biennials) — makes
47	a city swarm without producing a scheduling problem, because a months-long
48	exhibition has no performance times to clash.
49	
50	## The two close analogues
51	
52	### Adelaide — the only peer by scale
53	
54	Adelaide Fringe is the world's second-largest annual arts festival and is
55	explicitly open access ("welcomes anyone with an event to participate"). The 2026
56	edition ran **20 February – 22 March** with **1,648 shows across 562 venues** and
57	about **1,083,000 tickets** sold, part of more than six million attendances at
58	ticketed and free events.
59	
60	It shares the surrounding-cluster property too: the Adelaide Festival, WOMADelaide
61	and Writers' Week run alongside it, which is why locals call the period "Mad
62	March."
63	
64	Two structural differences that matter to the product:
65	
66	- **It is not one calendar month.** 20 Feb – 22 Mar spans two months. The
67	  planner's calendar axis is a single month.
68	- **562 venues to Edinburgh's 258**, in a city with a far less compact core —
69	  travel-time estimation is doing more work there, not less.
70	
71	### Avignon — the closest structural twin
72	
73	Avignon in July is the same *shape* as Edinburgh in August: a curated Festival
74	d'Avignon ("the IN") plus the open-access **Festival OFF**, inside a small walled
75	medieval town. The 60th OFF (**4–25 July 2026**) carried **1,780 shows in 141
76	theatres**, roughly **27,000 performances**, around 1,250 performances a day, from
77	~1,600 companies (about 90% French). Average auditorium fill was **54%** —
78	the same "too much supply chasing too little attention" economics as the Fringe.
79	
80	If any city is EdFringeNow's second market on structure alone, it is this one.
81	The blocker is not the model, it is that the entire corpus is in French.
82	
83	## Other potential candidate events
84	
85	The longer tail, grouped by which mechanism produces the crowd. Each is a
86	candidate, not a recommendation — none has been assessed for data accessibility
87	beyond what is noted.
88	
89	### Open-access fringes (same mechanism, smaller)
90	
91	There are **more than 300** fringe festivals worldwide in the World Fringe
92	network; Perth's own materials put the figure above 400. The count is large and
93	the tail is thin — only three sell over a quarter of a million tickets.
94	
95	- **Perth, Australia — FRINGE WORLD** (Jan–Feb). The third-largest fringe on the
96	  planet: **600+ shows across 110 venues** in 2026, ~3,000 artists, off **256,000
97	  tickets** sold in 2025.
98	- **Brighton, UK** (1–31 May). Open access, around **400,000 in-person
99	  attendances**, with over 30% of events from Brighton & Hove companies. English
100	  language, UK ticketing conventions — the cheapest possible second market.
101	- **Makhanda (Grahamstown), South Africa — National Arts Festival** (late
102	  June–July). **270+ productions** on the main programme in 2026 plus a Fringe of
103	  **200+ new works**, in a town small enough that the visitor-to-resident ratio may
104	  be the most extreme of any candidate here.
105	- **Toronto, Canada** (30 Jun – 12 Jul 2026). **123 shows**, selected by
106	  *lottery* rather than pure open access — a different supply mechanism, and small
107	  enough that overwhelm is not really the user's problem.
108	- Also in the network and unassessed: **Prague**, **Dublin**, **Winnipeg**,
109	  **Orlando**, **Minnesota**, **Wellington**, **Camden**, **Melbourne**.
110	
111	### Curated core plus an unofficial "off"
112	
113	- **Milan — Salone del Mobile / Fuorisalone** (April). The purest non-theatre
114	  version of the Edinburgh dynamic: a ticketed trade fair at Rho with 1,900+
115	  exhibitors, plus **1,100+ events listed on the official Fuorisalone guide
116	  (1,300+ across the city) spread over 16 districts** and **500,000+ visitors**.
117	  Brera alone carried 320 events across 217 showrooms. Installations run for the
118	  week rather than to performance times, so the *scheduling* problem is weaker
119	  than the *reachability* problem — which is the half of the product the Now page
120	  serves.
121	- **Charleston, SC — Spoleto Festival USA / Piccolo Spoleto** (late May–June).
122	  Piccolo Spoleto 2026 offered **250 events**, 190 of them produced by independent
123	  arts and community groups, 113 free — a deliberately open companion to a
124	  curated core, at a scale where a planner is plausible but not urgent.
125	- **Miami Beach — Art Basel plus satellite fairs** (December). Same shape,
126	  unassessed.
127	- **Cannes**, **SXSW Austin** (March). Both convert a city into temporary venues
128	  at high density with genuine clash-resolution problems, but both are
129	  trade/badge-driven rather than public-audience-driven, and SXSW already ships
130	  its own scheduling tool.
131	
132	### Festival seasons (many festivals, not one big one)
133	
134	- **Montreal** (summer). Festival International de Jazz de Montréal (25 Jun – 4
135	  Jul 2026) puts **350+ shows** and 3,000 performers in front of a claimed 2m+
136	  guests; Just For Laughs (15–26 Jul 2026) is the world's largest comedy festival
137	  with **250 shows across 25 downtown venues** and 800+ artists **in both official
138	  languages**. Concentrated in the Quartier des Spectacles, so reachability is
139	  real. Bilingual by default — the first candidate that forces the localization
140	  question.
141	- **Sibiu, Romania — FITS** (19–28 June 2026). **800+ events** in ten days in a
142	  small old town; one of Europe's largest performing-arts festivals.
143	- **Galway, Ireland — GIAF** (13–26 July 2026). Fourteen days, audiences well in
144	  excess of 200,000, in a small city fully consumed by it.
145	- **Salzburg, Austria** (17 Jul – 30 Aug 2026). **208 performances** across opera,
146	  drama and concerts. The town is overwhelmed, but the programme is curated,
147	  expensive and elite — 208 performances is a brochure, not an overwhelm problem.
148	  Included as the boundary case: *city swarming* alone is not the pattern.
149	
150	### Long exhibition runs (crowd without a clash problem)
151	
152	- **Venice — Biennale Arte** (9 May – 22 Nov 2026). **100 national
153	  participations** — 29 in the Giardini, 25 in the Arsenale and **46 scattered
154	  across the city** — plus **31 collateral events** in venues around Venice. A
155	  months-long run means opening hours, not performance times.
156	- **Kassel — Documenta** (every five years, 100 days) and the roving **Manifesta**
157	  are the same category, unassessed.
158	
159	## Where Edinburgh is still singular
160	
161	Two findings cut against expanding, and both should be said plainly:
162	
163	- **Nothing is close on density.** Edinburgh's Fringe alone is ~2.2× Adelaide on
164	  show count (3,649 vs 1,648, both 2026) and ~2.4× on tickets (2.6m in 2025 vs
165	  1.08m in 2026 — the newest full-year figure each publishes), in a smaller, more
166	  walkable centre, and it overlaps five other major festivals. The overwhelm the
167	  product exists to solve is genuinely worst here.
168	- **Edinburgh is the only candidate with an official aggregation layer.** The
169	  Edinburgh Festivals Listings API is a free API over the official listings
170	  database for all **11** Edinburgh festivals, carrying over **640,000
171	  performances**, with `events` and `venues` endpoints and a self-service access
172	  key. Its coverage, fields, licence terms and the two edges that matter (it is
173	  **availability-blind**, and its no-redistribution clause sits awkwardly with
174	  this repo's committed static data) are worked through on
175	  [festival-season/](../festival-season/README.md) and not repeated here. The
176	  point for *this* page is comparative: **no equivalent single-source feed was
177	  found for Adelaide, Avignon, Perth, Milan or Montreal** — those are
178	  per-festival scrapes or nothing. That asymmetry, not language, is the real cost
179	  of a second city.

input.body:
Weekly `wiki-growth` pass. This run's dispatch issue flagged that the product-wiki tree moved last week (the festival-season / fringe-ticketing / festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh pages landed 2026-07-31/08-01), so this pass spot-checked the two pages most affected by that wave — `competitor-landscape/` and `festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh/` — for citations time or that change may have superseded, on top of the normal open-questions triage.

## What changed and why

**`product-wiki/festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh/README.md`**
- The Perth FRINGE WORLD entry cited the still-upcoming 2026 edition's preview figures. That edition (21 Jan–15 Feb 2026) has since run and closed — this repo's clock is 2026-08-02 — and FRINGE WORLD's own about-us page now reports final results: 599 events, more than 3,000 artists, nearly 500,000 attendees, $10.9m spent at the Box Office ($8.34m to artists/venues), versus 2025's 570 events / 492,369 attendees / $10.78m. Added alongside the original preview figures (not a silent replacement) with an explicit note that "attendees" and "tickets sold" are different metrics, so this does not resolve the page's existing 256,000-tickets figure.
- Narrowed (did not close) the "Perth cites 400+ fringes, World Fringe cites 300+" open question with FRINGE WORLD's own exact wording ("a global landscape of more than 400 Fringe festivals") — a broader claim than a stated network-membership count, which is plausibly what the two figures are each counting, but neither site states its methodology.

**`product-wiki/competitor-landscape/README.md`**
- Re-ran the "is anything actually planning across festivals?" open question. Surfaced two 2026 entrants not previously profiled: FringePlan (Fringe-only day planner, close to Plan My Fringe/Plan Your Fringe) and planmyfestivals.com, whose plural "Festival[s]" naming is the first candidate found whose own branding suggests cross-festival scope. Neither was fetched or examined hands-on (WebFetch 403'd on both), so planmyfestivals.com's actual scope stays an open question, not a finding.
- `## Key insights` header on both pages left unchanged — neither finding changes either page's top-line read.

## Citations added
- FRINGE WORLD about-us (fringeworld.com.au/about-us) — the 400+ fringes wording and the 2026 final results
- FringePlan (fringeplan.com)
- planmyfestivals.com

## Open questions left for the next run
- planmyfestivals.com's actual scope (Fringe-only vs cross-festival) — unconfirmed, WebFetch blocked on it this run
- The 400+ vs 300+ fringes count is narrowed but still not reconciled
- Everything else already open on both pages is untouched

No `product-wiki/product-requirements/` changes; no requirements implications from this pass.

This run's dispatch issue flagged that the product-wiki tree moved last week (the festival-season / fringe-ticketing / festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh pages landed 2026-07-31/08-01), so this pass spot-checked the two pages most affected by that wave — `competitor-landscape/` and `festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh/` — for citations time or that change may have superseded, on top of the normal open-questions triage.

## What changed and why

**`product-wiki/festival-cities-beyond-edinburgh/README.md`**
- The Perth FRINGE WORLD entry cited the still-upcoming 2026 edition's preview figures. That edition (21 Jan–15 Feb 2026) has since run and closed — this repo's clock is 2026-08-02 — and FRINGE WORLD's own about-us page now reports final results: 599 events, more than 3,000 artists, nearly 500,000 attendees, $10.9m spent at the Box Office ($8.34m to artists/venues), versus 2025's 570 events / 492,369 attendees / $10.78m. Added alongside the original preview figures (not a silent replacement) with an explicit note that "attendees" and "tickets sold" are different metrics, so this does not resolve the page's existing 256,000-tickets figure.
- Narrowed (did not close) the "Perth cites 400+ fringes, World Fringe cites 300+" open question with FRINGE WORLD's own exact wording ("a global landscape of more than 400 Fringe festivals") — a broader claim than a stated network-membership count, which is plausibly what the two figures are each counting, but neither site states its methodology.

**`product-wiki/competitor-landscape/README.md`**
- Re-ran the "is anything actually planning across festivals?" open question. Surfaced two 2026 entrants not previously profiled: FringePlan (Fringe-only day planner, close to Plan My Fringe/Plan Your Fringe) and planmyfestivals.com, whose plural "Festival[s]" naming is the first candidate found whose own branding suggests cross-festival scope. Neither was fetched or examined hands-on (WebFetch 403'd on both), so planmyfestivals.com's actual scope stays an open question, not a finding.
- `## Key insights` header on both pages left unchanged — neither finding changes either page's top-line read.

## Citations added
- FRINGE WORLD about-us (fringeworld.com.au/about-us) — the 400+ fringes wording and the 2026 final results
- FringePlan (fringeplan.com)
- planmyfestivals.com

## Open questions left for the next run
- planmyfestivals.com's actual scope (Fringe-only vs cross-festival) — unconfirmed, WebFetch blocked on it this run
- The 400+ vs 300+ fringes count is narrowed but still not reconciled
- Everything else already open on both pages is untouched

No `product-wiki/product-requirements/` changes; no requirements implications from this pass.
